Detect-and-reweight methods suppress likely-synthetic samples during pretraining via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$, where $q(x)$ is a detector's synthetic probability.
Two questions are open: does hard filtering (Detect and Remove, D\&R) outperform soft reweighting, and how should $b$ be set without per-model grid search?

We address both through controlled experiments in a self-contamination setting: Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining on 132M FineWeb tokens with 40\% synthetic contamination (3 seeds).
First, D\&R's reported advantage is entirely a multi-epoch artifact: at equal content epochs, reweighting and D\&R differ by only 0.006 perplexity (PPL; $N{=}3$).
Second, the in-distribution PPL improvement from adaptive reweighting does not transfer to out-of-distribution corpora (OpenWebText, Wikipedia), consistent with distribution matching rather than general quality gain.
Third, a dual-constrained adaptive $b^*$ improves over uniform weighting on in-distribution evaluation with directional consistency across all seeds (95\% confidence interval (CI) of the adaptive-to-grid gap includes possible degradation up to 0.10 PPL); our results suggest detector signal type may matter more than discrimination accuracy (3 detectors, single seed).

The method fails at low contamination ($\rho{=}0.2$), which establishes a clear applicability boundary.
$N{=}3$ precludes formal significance testing; we report effect sizes and directional consistency.
tool_args.new_string:
As synthetic text reaches an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora, detect-and-reweight methods that downweight likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$ have gained traction.
Two questions remain open: does hard filtering outperform soft reweighting, and how should the exponent $b$ be set without per-model grid search?

Through controlled experiments (Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining, 132M FineWeb tokens, 40\% contamination, 3 seeds), we identify two confounds in current evaluation practice.
Detect and Remove (D\&R) owes its reported advantage entirely to multi-epoch exposure: at matched content epochs, D\&R and reweighting differ by only 0.006 perplexity ($N{=}3$).
In-distribution perplexity gains from adaptive reweighting do not transfer out-of-distribution (OpenWebText $+$0.06, Wikipedia $+$0.14), consistent with distribution matching rather than general quality improvement.
A dual-constrained adaptive $b^*$, selecting the minimum exponent that satisfies a quality floor while preserving gradient stability, matches grid-search performance without per-model tuning (gap 0.031, within seed variance $\pm$0.033); detector signal type appears to matter more than discrimination accuracy (3 detectors, single seed).
The method fails at $\rho{=}0.2$ and shows no effect at 1.7B; with $N{=}3$, we report effect sizes and directional consistency rather than formal significance.

The in-distribution PPL improvement reverses out-of-distribution ($+$0.06 OpenWebText, $+$0.14 Wikipedia; seed 42, other-seed checkpoints not retained), consistent with distribution matching rather than general improvement.
This pattern likely affects all contamination-aware reweighting that upweights human-authored samples~\citep{drayson2025detection}: in-distribution PPL may be an inadequate metric for evaluating contamination mitigation, since any method that shifts the training distribution toward the evaluation distribution will show gains regardless of genuine quality improvement.
Given this caveat, the concrete benefit of adaptive $\bstar$ is operational: reducing grid search from nine runs to one (${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B).

Our empirical analysis of contamination-aware reweighting in continued pretraining identifies two evaluation confounds and characterizes when adaptive reweighting is effective.
First, D\&R's reported advantage over soft reweighting is entirely attributable to multi-epoch exposure ($\Delta{=}0.006$ at equal content epochs, $N{=}3$; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
Second, the in-distribution PPL improvement does not transfer to out-of-distribution corpora, consistent with distribution matching rather than general quality gain.
Third, dual-constrained adaptive $\bstar$ improves in-distribution PPL over uniform weighting ($\rho \in \{0.4, 0.6\}$, directionally consistent across seeds) and reduces $b$ grid search to a single default $\tau$; detector signal type may matter more than discrimination accuracy (3 detectors, single seed).
The method fails at $\rho{=}0.2$, and at 1.7B we find no evidence of improvement or degradation ($\Delta{=}{-}0.01$, 2 seeds).
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
tool_args.new_string:
This analysis identifies two evaluation confounds in contamination-aware reweighting (epoch exposure and distribution matching) and characterizes when adaptive $\bstar$ is effective ($\rho \geq 0.4$ with a discriminative detector).
The most broadly relevant finding is that in-distribution PPL improvement does not transfer out-of-distribution: contamination-aware reweighting may function as distribution correction rather than quality improvement, a distinction that affects how such methods should be evaluated.
The adaptive framework's practical contribution is replacing per-model $b$ grid search with a single default $\tau$, though the effect size is modest ($\Delta{=}{-}0.043$ at $\rho{=}0.4$) and absent at 1.7B ($\Delta{=}{-}0.01$, 2 seeds).
Future work should establish evaluation protocols that distinguish genuine quality gains from distribution-shift artifacts, and test whether adaptive reweighting transfers beyond continued pretraining to web-scale settings.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
